body.text: The Afghan Taliban is not attending the U.N. Climate Change Conference (COP31) ongoing in Turkiye as they did not receive a formal invitation. They attended COP29 in Baku, Azerbaijan, in 2024 for the first time and participated as observers. However, the group was not invited to COP30, which was held in Brazil in 2025, and it was not invited to COP31 in Turkiye.

The absence of a Taliban delegation at the climate summit excludes Afghanistan from formal participation in global climate negotiations, despite being one of the countries most vulnerable to the devastating impacts of climate change.

Over the past several years, constantly increasing temperatures, recurrent droughts, erratic rainfall and floods, compounding water scarcity, land degradation and environmental decline have intensified in Afghanistan. According to Afghanistan’s National Environmental Protection Agency, temperatures rose by 1.8 degrees Celsius between 1950 and 2010, twice the global average. Subsequent floods, droughts, avalanches, and snowstorms affect approximately 200,000 people every year. These environmental pressures are further complicated by decades of conflict, poverty, weak infrastructure, and limited access to basic services. The climate crisis in Afghanistan requires immediate attention.

Afghanistan’s environmental crisis is not simply a result of climate change or geographical vulnerability; it is also a crisis of governance. In 2021, the Afghan Taliban took control of a country devastated by decades of war and institutional weakness, but the group’s own policies, restrictive political practices, and failure to establish an inclusive environmental framework have further aggravated the country’s problems.

The first environmental step the Afghan Taliban took after their return to power in 2021 was announcing a ban on the timber trade. Taliban spokesperson Zabihullah Mujahid issued a tweet stating that cutting down forests, as well as selling or transporting timber, would be strictly prohibited. Then, in December 2021, Taliban officials announced the creation of the Green Unit, a special military unit tasked solely with protecting Afghanistan’s forests from illegal logging. Recently, they set a goal of planting 200 million trees between 2023 and 2030 with the help of the international community.

Notably, Afghanistan does not have a dedicated ministry of climate; instead, environmental and climate policies are overseen by the National Environmental Protection Agency (NEPA) and the Ministry of Agriculture, Irrigation and Livestock (MAIL). NEPA has been headed by Mati-ul-Haq Khalis since July 2024.

Afghanistan’s climate crisis has two important dimensions: accelerating desertification and deforestation. More than 75 percent of land in northern, western and southern Afghanistan is affected by desertification, caused by prolonged and recurrent droughts, declining groundwater reserves and increasingly unpredictable precipitation patterns.

As a 2021 U.N. Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) report noted, “Agriculture is the backbone of Afghan livelihoods and critical for Afghanistan’s economy.” The report stated that approximately 70 percent of Afghanistan’s population resides in rural areas and agriculture contributes at least 25 percent of the country’s GDP. “[A]n estimated 80 percent of all livelihoods depend directly or indirectly on agriculture,” the FAO said.

Successive droughts have reduced crop yields, destroyed pasturelands, and intensified food insecurity. Meanwhile, environmental degradation and drought intensify competition over land and water, heightening social and economic tensions within and between communities and undermining social cohesion.

The Afghan Taliban have yet to prepare a comprehensive and adequately funded national strategy capable of addressing these interconnected threats. Their response has largely remained fragmented, reactive and dependent on humanitarian assistance provided by the international donor community rather than a coherent program of climate adaptation and environmental resilience.

Deforestation is another serious aspect of the ecological challenges in Afghanistan. Widespread poverty and the absence of affordable energy alternatives force millions of Afghans to depend on firewood and coal for cooking and heating. This dependence places enormous pressure on already fragile forests and natural vegetation.

The problem is compounded by weak environmental regulation, limited enforcement and inadequate investment in renewable energy. Although the Green Unit played some role in discouraging illegal logging, their enforcement mechanism remains largely inconsistent. The economic desperation of common Afghans continues to encourage unsustainable practices. Environmental protection cannot succeed through prohibitions alone; it requires affordable energy, alternative livelihoods, and community participation, none of which have received sufficient institutional attention by the Afghan Taliban.

The Afghan Taliban’s approach to natural resource management further exposes the weaknesses of its environmental policies. Unregulated coal extraction and illegal mining threaten ecosystems, water resources, and public health. Coal may provide short-term economic revenue and energy, but uncontrolled extraction carries substantial environmental costs, including land degradation, air pollution, and contamination of water sources.

The country’s worsening water crisis is perhaps the clearest illustration of the gap between environmental needs and the capacity of the Afghan Taliban to handle the climate crisis. Afghanistan’s rivers, groundwater systems, and traditional irrigation networks are under growing pressure from drought, population needs, and changing climate conditions. Large-scale investment in the construction of small dams, rainwater reservoirs, modern irrigation, and groundwater management is urgently required. However, international isolation and loss of development assistance have severely restricted resources. For example, in 2022 Taliban authorities claimed that the international community withheld funding for 32 environmental protection projects worth $805 million.

A fundamental weakness in this regard is the absence of inclusive and accountable environmental governance led by the Afghan Taliban. Afghanistan requires cooperation between local communities, agricultural experts, environmental scientists, civil society organizations, and international development institutions. Instead, centralized decision-making, restrictions on independent institutions, and the marginalization of women and professional groups have weakened the country’s capacity to formulate and implement effective environmental policies. Climate resilience cannot be imposed from above; it requires public participation, reliable information, institutional accountability, and the protection of local communities’ rights.

The international community also has a responsibility to prevent Afghanistan’s environmental crisis from becoming an irreversible humanitarian tragedy. Political disagreements with the Afghan Taliban should not result in the abandonment of millions of Afghans confronting drought, hunger, and severe food security crisis. Approximately 40 percent of the population of Afghanistan is projected to face high levels of acute food insecurity in 2026.

Afghanistan needs an environmental policy based on a combination of scientific evidence, sustainable resource management, transparent administration, and international cooperation, which requires both political will and capacity on the part of the Taliban regime. Unless the Afghan Taliban acknowledge climate security as a national priority, desertification, water scarcity, deforestation, and climate-induced displacement will continue to threaten Afghan people in both rural and urban areas. For a nation already struggling with poverty and political isolation, environmental misgovernance is not merely a policy failure; rather it is a threat to national survival.
